Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa promised to freeze residential electricity rates on Day One. She told the Texas Tribune she'd declare a "high-cost emergency" within an hour of taking office Jan. 19, then have the state freeze home rates until data centers and other big users pay their own way. Texas homes paid 15.91 cents per kWh in August vs. 18.16 cents nationally (U.S. EIA). Supporters say families need relief now. Critics say price caps in a competitive market could discourage new power plants and end up in court. Promise status: not started. Sources: Texas Tribune via Fox News and Energy Choice Matters, U.S. EIA.

Texas is 1 of 10 states that haven't expanded Medicaid. Bills filed Monday aim to change that.

On Nov. 9, the first day of 2027 bill filing, Rep. John Bucy (D-Austin) filed HB 101 and HB 102, and Sen. Judith Zaffirini (D-Laredo) filed SB 31. They would direct the state's health agency to expand Medicaid to more low-income adults. The Texas Tribune reports expansion could cover about 1 million more Texans and bring the state up to $10 billion a year. The federal government generally pays 90% of costs for newly eligible adults.

Who decides: Democrats will run the House. Republicans, who have blocked expansion and argue it would be wasteful, still hold the Senate. Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa would sign or veto. The session starts Jan. 12.

Why it matters: 16.5% of Texans were uninsured in 2025, about double the U.S. rate of 8.4%.

What should lawmakers know about health coverage where you live?

Sources: The Texas Tribune, Texas Public Radio, Dallas Express (links in the first comment)

Some local Texas races aren't over: runoffs are Dec. 12.

Some local races from the Nov. 3 election, for offices like city councils, school boards and water districts, are headed to a runoff. The Texas Secretary of State has set Saturday, Dec. 12, 2026 as the date for runoffs from those local elections.

Key dates for the Dec. 12 runoff:
• Nov. 12: last day to register to vote or change your address
• Nov. 30 to Dec. 8: early voting
• Dec. 12: runoff election day

Only places with a local runoff on the ballot hold a Dec. 12 election. These dates come from the state's official runoff election calendar.

Filed isn't passed: what Texas Democrats proposed this week

Bill filing for the 2027 Texas legislative session opened Nov. 9, and Democrats pre-filed bills on several big issues:

• Expand Medicaid (House bill by Rep. John Bucy, Senate bill by Sen. Judith Zaffirini)
• Raise the state minimum wage to $15 an hour (HB 110, HB 132)
• Legalize, tax and regulate marijuana (HB 362, HB 369)
• Raise the minimum age to buy certain semi-automatic rifles to 21 (HB 173)

These are proposals, not laws. A bill has to pass the Texas House and Senate and get past the governor. Democrats now hold the House; Republicans still hold the Senate, where the Texas Tribune expects many of these ideas to face heavy resistance. Republicans filed their own bills too, including ones to cut or end property taxes.

You may have seen "20 gun bills." So far we could confirm the rifle-age bill only.

Which should we track?

Sources: Texas Tribune, Marijuana Moment (links in the first comment)

Will it change what you pay? Hinojosa's promise to freeze home electricity rates

On the campaign trail, Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) promised: "On Day One as governor, I'll freeze residential electricity rates and make corporations finally pay their fair share."

What she says she'll do:
• Declare a "high-cost emergency" within an hour of taking the oath on Jan. 19, she told the Texas Tribune. She said the same order would also suspend the state gas and diesel tax.
• Have the Public Utility Commission freeze residential rates until new laws make data centers and other high-load users pay for their own power.

Where prices stand: the average Texas home paid 15.91 cents per kilowatt-hour in August 2026, up from 15.40 cents a year earlier. The U.S. average was 18.16 cents. (U.S. EIA)

The open questions: Most Texans buy power from competing retail providers whose prices the state doesn't set, so how a freeze would work isn't clear yet. Lasting changes would need the Legislature, and Republicans still hold the Texas Senate.

How each side sees it:
Supporters say data centers are pushing up household bills and families need relief now.
Critics, including Nick Loris of the conservative group C3 Solutions in a Fox News story, say capping prices in a competitive market could discourage new power supply and will likely be challenged in court.

Promise status: not started. She takes office Jan. 19, 2027, and we'll track whether the freeze happens and holds up.

Should a governor be able to freeze electricity rates? Tell us below.
